opus-5.5.text:
I think in that window, roughly 2017 to 2020, quadrupeds hit a kind of sweet spot that's easy to underestimate in hindsight.

First, the hardware suddenly became accessible. Before that, legged robots meant big hydraulic machines like the early Boston Dynamics platforms: very impressive, but expensive, fragile, and hard for a university lab to own. Then you had the MIT Cheetah line showing that proprioceptive actuators, basically high-torque electric motors with low gear ratios, could make a robot that was dynamic, robust to impacts, and much cheaper. Once that design philosophy spread, you got platforms like ANYmal, Minitaur, and later the Unitree robots, and suddenly a grad student could have a legged robot on the desk and fall it over a hundred times a day without it being a disaster.

Second, quadrupeds are statically and dynamically a forgiving body. Compared with humanoids, four legs give you a much larger support polygon, so failures are less catastrophic and you can iterate faster. But it's still a genuinely hard control problem: contact-rich, hybrid dynamics, underactuated during flight phases. So it's hard enough to be interesting, yet tractable enough that you can actually make progress and see it on a real robot.

Third, and I think this is the big one, the timing lined up with learning-based control. Deep RL had worked in games and in simulation, and people were asking whether it could ever transfer to real hardware. Locomotion turned out to be the perfect test case. The reward is relatively easy to specify, simulators like PyBullet, MuJoCo, and later Isaac Gym were getting good enough, and with tricks like domain randomization and actuator modeling, the sim-to-real gap became bridgeable. Work from ETH, Google, Berkeley, and others showed policies trained in simulation walking on real robots over rough terrain. That was a very visible, very convincing demonstration that learning could do something classical model-based control struggled with.

And finally, there's an intuitive appeal. When you see a robot dog recover from a kick or walk over snow, everyone immediately understands it. You don't need to explain the benchmark. That made it great for attracting students, funding, and attention.

So, to me, quadrupeds in that period were less about "we need robot dogs" and more about having a clean, affordable, physically real testbed where the question "can learning actually control a body in the real world?" could finally be answered. And in many ways the answer was yes, which is part of why the field later felt confident moving on to humanoids and manipulation.

r001.rationale: The response says quadrupeds became affordable and accessible to university labs, but it does not compare their accessibility with robot arms.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it, quadrupeds around 2017 to 2020 hit a sweet spot that very few platforms hit at the same time.

The first thing is that the hardware had finally become accessible. Before that, if you wanted to work on legged locomotion, you were basically looking at Boston Dynamics-class machines that cost as much as a house, or you were building your own actuators from scratch. Then you had the MIT Cheetah work, the open-sourced Mini Cheetah design, Unitree starting to ship things at a price a university lab could actually justify, ANYmal coming out of ETH. Suddenly a grad student could have a real legged robot on a bench. That changes everything about who gets to work on the problem.

The second thing is that a quadruped is hard enough to be interesting, but not so hard that you spend all your time just keeping it from falling over. A biped is brutal. Every step is a controlled fall. A quadruped has a bigger support polygon, it can stand statically, it's forgiving. So you can ask the real question, which is how do you get a legged system to move robustly over terrain that wheels can't handle, without the balance problem eating your entire PhD.

And the third thing, which I think is the one that really drove the explosion, is timing with learning. Right around then, reinforcement learning was going from "works in simulation on Atari" to "maybe this transfers to physical systems." Quadrupeds turned out to be an almost perfect testbed for sim-to-real. The dynamics are rich enough that hand-tuned model predictive controllers hit a ceiling, especially on rough or unknown terrain. But the robot is robust enough that when your policy does something stupid, you don't destroy a hundred-thousand-dollar machine. You pick it up and run it again. The ETH work on learning agile locomotion and then walking in the wild really showed people that this loop could close, and after that it felt like every lab wanted one.

There's also a softer thing, which is that a walking robot is just legible. You show someone a dog-shaped thing walking over rocks and they immediately get it. Funders get it, students get it, the public gets it. You don't have to explain why it matters. That's not nothing when you're trying to build a research program.

So I'd say the appeal was the convergence: cheap enough hardware, a problem that was tractable but unsolved, and a new set of tools in learning that needed exactly that kind of platform to prove themselves on.

r001.rationale: The response says quadruped hardware became accessible to university labs, but it does not compare that accessibility with robot arms.

astra-6.text:
I think the appeal was that quadrupeds brought a lot of difficult robotics problems together in one platform. You had to deal with balance, contact with the ground, planning, and control—and all of those things had to work together in real time. You couldn’t just solve each piece independently and assume the robot would walk.

Four legs also gave you a useful balance between stability and complexity. You could explore dynamic movement and uneven terrain, while still having more options for supporting the body than you would with two legs. So it was a compelling platform for asking how robots could move beyond very structured environments.

And the results were very tangible. If you improved an algorithm, you could see the robot recover from a push or negotiate an obstacle. Around that period, I think that combination of scientific depth and visible progress made quadrupeds especially attractive.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes quadrupeds as useful and compelling research platforms, but does not compare their hardware accessibility with robot arms.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the appeal was that quadrupeds brought together a lot of difficult robotics problems in one platform. You had to deal with dynamics, balance, contact with the ground, and real-time control. And once you wanted the robot to move beyond a controlled lab environment, perception and planning became essential too.

Around 2017 to 2020, they also felt increasingly practical as research platforms. You could start asking not just, “Can we make this machine walk?” but, “Can it adapt to different terrain? Can it recover from a disturbance? Can it learn a useful behavior?” That made them interesting to people working on both traditional control and learning.

And there’s a very intuitive appeal: when you see a four-legged robot keep its balance or negotiate an obstacle, you immediately understand the challenge. It makes fairly abstract research questions tangible.

r001.rationale: The response describes quadrupeds as increasingly practical research platforms, but does not compare their hardware accessibility with robot arms or suggest they were more accessible.
